name: Phyla

project_scope.note: Single-species genus study lesson uses identified neighboring taxa as references, not learner-approved new species. No new canonical species or nativity changes.

genus_recognition.look_here_first: Frogfruit forms creeping ROOTING-NODE mats with opposite leaves whose widest point and teeth are usually near the TIP. Then find a tiny button-to-cylinder spike of minute flowers on a long bare AXILLARY stalk; do not confuse with terminal Verbena/Glandularia flower heads.
genus_recognition.source_order: habit → leaf/stem architecture → flower structure → fruit/seed → specialist comparison

visual_id_sequence: 1. Inspect entire plant habit and growth form.
2. Zoom to stem node and complete mature leaf with ruler.
3. Inspect close flower and reproductive parts, labeling all structures rather than flower color alone.
4. Confirm mature fruit architecture with macro and seed view.
5. Compare the nearest confuser against matched structural photos; keep ambiguous IDs at genus.

visual_comparison.title: Frogfruit — read the leaf, rooting node, and axillary flower head
visual_comparison.subtitle: Three installed real Phyla nodiflora photographs. This is a field-recognition sequence, not a licensed matched-species comparison or a final key to all Phyla species.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: ROOTING RUNNER + OPPOSITE LEAVES + TINY FLOWERS IN AN AXILLARY BUTTON = PHYLA. For NODIFLORA, check MANY leaves: distal teeth and a blade often broadest above its midpoint.

items.label: 1 — Leaf teeth and shape
items.image_role: Mature opposite leaves; inspect blade outline and where teeth begin
items.caption: Look at several fully expanded leaves. P. nodiflora commonly has a blade broadest beyond the midpoint and teeth concentrated toward its tip. Variation means this alone cannot separate P. lanceolata.
items.creator: Forest & Kim Starr

items.label: 2 — Creeping mat and rooting stem
items.caption: Start with the growth form. Follow a stem along the soil and look for roots developing at nodes; confirm opposite leaves. Rooting nodes are diagnostic for habit but not enough alone for species.
items.creator: Dinesh Valke

items.label: 3 — Axillary flower-head architecture
items.image_role: Tiny flowers densely crowded into buttonlike to elongating head
items.caption: Follow the long mostly leafless stalk back to the leaf axil where it originates. The dense head of minute flowers is very different from the larger, more open terminal flower clusters of Glandularia.
items.creator: yating
items.photo_status: PHYSICAL_IMAGE_PRESENT; PRIVATE STUDY ONLY pending public-use license approval

quick_field_decision: Find the leaf axil and identify where the flower-head stalk emerges; do not infer an axillary origin from a cropped head alone.
Check 3–5 mature leaves on different nodes for the position of greatest width and teeth distribution.
Find the long creeping stems and inspect nodes for roots.
If a closely related Phyla has overlapping leaf shape, record Phyla sp. until the calyx, floral parts, and mature fruit can be compared.
science_cautions: P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia are documented comparison references, not canonical learner species; do not claim side-by-side matched images are already installed.
Three installed P. nodiflora photos demonstrate different roles but may not each resolve all micro-diagnostic structures.
Third image has a CC BY-NC attribution; do not republish outside permitted noncommercial uses without rights review.
